motion-quantities-s1.title: A cart rolls up a ramp and back
motion-quantities-s1.text: A student gives a cart a quick push up a long, straight ramp and lets go at t = 0. A motion detector at the bottom of the ramp records the cart's velocity, with up the ramp as positive.

table.caption: Velocity of the cart after release

motion-quantities-s2.title: Four cars on a straight road
motion-quantities-s2.text: Each car is shown at one instant, with its velocity (v, gold) and its acceleration (a, red). Right is positive. Each car's acceleration stays the same for the next few seconds.
motion-quantities-s2.html: Key: gold arrow, velocity v; red arrow, acceleration a. Right is positive. Arrows show directions, not sizes.

motion-quantities-s3.title: A ball rolling down a ramp, timed closely
motion-quantities-s3.text: A ball is released from rest at t = 0 and rolls down a long ramp. A video tracker gives its position along the ramp at the times below.

table.caption: Position of the ball along the ramp

items.q: The cart's velocity changes by the same amount in each 0.5 s interval. What is its acceleration at t = 1.5 s, the instant its velocity is zero?
options: Zero, because the cart is momentarily at rest
The same as at the other readings: negative, not zero
Positive, because the cart is about to turn around
It is undefined, because Δt is zero at a single instant

why.correct: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, not the velocity. From 1.0 s to 2.0 s the velocity goes +0.40 → −0.40 m/s, the same steady change as before, including at the instant v = 0.
options: A zero velocity is not a zero acceleration. The velocity is still changing at that instant: it was positive and becomes negative.
Right: the velocity keeps changing by −0.40 m/s every 0.5 s, straight through zero, so the acceleration has not changed.
The velocity goes from positive to negative, so Δv is negative; the acceleration does not flip sign at the top.
The table shows the same steady change before and after 1.5 s, so the acceleration there has the same value as at the other readings.

items.q: What is the cart's average acceleration from t = 0 to t = 1.0 s? Give a signed value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the size is right, but Δv is final minus initial, 0.40 − 1.20, which is negative.

why.correct: a = Δv/Δt = (0.40 m/s − 1.20 m/s) ÷ (1.0 s − 0) = −0.80 m/s². The minus sign: the acceleration points down the ramp.

items.q: From t = 1.5 s to t = 2.5 s, the cart rolls back down the ramp. During this time its acceleration is negative. What is happening to its speed?
options: It decreases, because a negative acceleration means slowing down
It stays the same, because the acceleration does not change
It decreases, because the velocity values are below zero
It increases, because the velocity and acceleration have the same sign

why.correct: Speeding up: velocity and acceleration point the same way. Slowing down: they point opposite ways. Here both are negative after 1.5 s, so the cart speeds up down the ramp.
options: Negative only gives a direction. Slowing down happens when acceleration and velocity have opposite signs.
A steady acceleration means the velocity changes steadily; the speed goes from 0 to 0.80 m/s.
The speed is the size of the velocity: 0.40 then 0.80 m/s, which is growing.
Right: both are negative, so the velocity grows more negative and the speed (its size) grows from 0 to 0.80 m/s.

items.q: What is the cart's change in velocity, Δv, from t = 0 to t = 2.5 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 0.40 m/s treats the two speeds as if they were in the same direction. Subtract with signs: −0.80 − (+1.20) = −2.00 m/s.
Value: you dropped the minus sign of the final velocity. The cart is moving down the ramp at 2.5 s, so v(final) = −0.80 m/s.

why.correct: Δv = v(final) − v(initial) = (−0.80 m/s) − (+1.20 m/s) = −2.00 m/s.

items.q: The ramp keeps going and the pattern continues. What velocity will the detector read at t = 3.5 s?

options: This adds only one more step of −0.40 m/s; 3.5 s is two half-second steps after 2.5 s.
Right: the velocity changes by −0.40 m/s each 0.5 s, so two more steps after −0.80 m/s give −1.60 m/s.
This assumes the cart turns back up the ramp; nothing in the data reverses the steady change.
This assumes the velocity stops changing, but the acceleration is the same at every reading.

items.q: Which car has a negative acceleration and is speeding up?
options: Car 3
Car 2
Car 4
Car 1

why.correct: Speeding up means v and a point the same way. Only car 3 has both pointing in the negative direction.
options: Right: its velocity and acceleration both point left (negative), so its speed grows.
Car 2 has a negative acceleration, but its velocity is positive, so it is slowing down.
Car 4 has a positive acceleration, opposite to its leftward velocity, so it is slowing down.
Car 1 is speeding up, but its acceleration points right, so it is positive.

items.q: Car 2 has a velocity of +12 m/s and an acceleration of −3.0 m/s². What is its velocity 2.0 s later?

mistakes.why: Value: 18 m/s adds the change, but the acceleration points opposite to the velocity, so Δv is −6.0 m/s.
Value: −6.0 m/s is Δv, the change. Add it to the starting velocity of +12 m/s.

why.correct: From a = Δv/Δt, Δv = aΔt = (−3.0 m/s²)(2.0 s) = −6.0 m/s. New velocity = +12 m/s + (−6.0 m/s) = +6.0 m/s: still moving right, but slower.

items.q: Car 4 has a velocity of −8.0 m/s and an acceleration of +2.0 m/s². What is its speed 1.5 s later?

mistakes.why: Value: 11 m/s adds 3.0 to the speed. The acceleration points opposite to the velocity, so the car slows: 8.0 − 3.0 = 5.0 m/s.
Value: −5.0 m/s is the velocity. The speed is its size, with no sign.

why.correct: Δv = aΔt = (+2.0 m/s²)(1.5 s) = +3.0 m/s. v = −8.0 m/s + 3.0 m/s = −5.0 m/s. The speed is the size: 5.0 m/s.

items.q: Car 1 and car 3 have accelerations of the same size. What is true of both cars over the next second?
options: Car 1 speeds up and car 3 slows down
Both speed up by the same amount
Both slow down, because their accelerations point in opposite directions
Neither changes speed, because their accelerations cancel

why.correct: For each car, compare its own v and a. Car 1: both right; car 3: both left. Both speed up, at the same rate.
options: Car 3's negative acceleration matches its negative velocity, so car 3 speeds up as well.
Right: in each car a points along v, so each speed grows, by the same amount because the accelerations have equal size.
Comparing the two cars' directions with each other says nothing; compare each car's a with its own v.
The cars are separate; one car's acceleration does not act on the other.

items.q: What is the ball's average velocity from 2.0 s to 3.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 1.2 m/s divides the final position by the final time. Use the changes: Δx ÷ Δt.

items.q: What is the ball's average velocity from 2.0 s to 2.1 s?

mistakes.why: Value: 0.84 m/s divides a position by a clock reading. Average velocity uses the change in position over the change in time.
Value: 0.164 m is the displacement; divide it by the 0.1 s interval.

why.correct: v(avg) = (1.764 m − 1.600 m) ÷ (2.1 s − 2.0 s) = 0.164 m ÷ 0.1 s = 1.64 m/s, about 1.6 m/s (Δt = 0.1 s has one or two significant figures; two is reasonable).

items.q: The average velocities from 2.0 s to 3.0 s, to 2.5 s and to 2.1 s are 2.0, 1.8 and 1.64 m/s. What is the best estimate of the ball's instantaneous velocity at exactly 2.0 s?
options: 2.0 m/s, because the longest interval uses the most data
About 1.8 m/s, the middle of the three values
About 1.6 m/s, the value the shrinking intervals approach
0.80 m/s, the position at 2.0 s divided by the time

why.correct: An instantaneous velocity is the average velocity over a very short interval. As Δt shrinks (1.0 → 0.5 → 0.1 s), the averages approach about 1.6 m/s.
options: Over a long interval the ball keeps speeding up, so that average includes later, faster motion.
The averages are moving steadily toward a value; the middle one is not special.
Right: the shorter the interval starting at 2.0 s, the closer its average is to the velocity at 2.0 s.
Position over clock time is not a velocity at an instant; it ignores how the position is changing.

items.q: What does the data show about the ball's motion between 2.0 s and 3.0 s?
options: It moves at a steady velocity, since the position increases each time
It is speeding up, since later equal intervals cover more distance
It is slowing down, since the average velocity gets smaller for shorter intervals
It is at rest at 2.0 s, since the ball started from rest

why.correct: Equal half-second intervals: 2.500 − 1.600 = 0.900 m, then 3.600 − 2.500 = 1.100 m. More distance in each later interval means the ball is speeding up.
options: Increasing position only shows the direction. A steady velocity would cover equal distances in equal times.
Right: 2.0 to 2.5 s covers 0.900 m, and 2.5 to 3.0 s covers 1.100 m, so the velocity is increasing.
The shorter intervals sit earlier in the motion, when the ball is slower; that shows it speeds up over time.
The ball started from rest at t = 0, not at 2.0 s; by 2.0 s it is already moving.

items.q: A sprinter starts from rest and reaches 9.0 m/s in 1.8 s. What is her average acceleration?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied. Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval.
Value: the fraction is upside down. Acceleration is Δv ÷ Δt, in (m/s)/s = m/s².

items.q: A delivery van drives 12.0 km east in 10.0 min, then 4.0 km west in 5.0 min. What is the size of its average velocity for the whole trip, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: about 18 m/s is the average speed, total distance over time. Average velocity uses the displacement, 8.0 km east.
Value: you divided by 15 minutes without converting. 15.0 min = 900 s.
Value: about 17 m/s averages the two legs' speeds (20 and 13 m/s). That drops the direction of the second leg and ignores that the legs last different times. Use total displacement ÷ total time.
Value: 3.3 m/s averages the two legs' velocities (+20 and −13 m/s), but the legs last different times. Use total displacement ÷ total time.

why.correct: Displacement = +12.0 km − 4.0 km = +8.0 km = 8000 m. Δt = 15.0 min = 900 s. v(avg) = 8000 m ÷ 900 s = 8.9 m/s (east).

items.q: Two bikes each gain 6.0 m/s of velocity. Bike A takes 3.0 s and bike B takes 1.5 s. How does bike B's average acceleration compare with bike A's?
options: Half as large
The same, because both gain 6.0 m/s
Twice as large
Four times as large

why.correct: a = Δv/Δt: 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 m/s² and 6.0/1.5 = 4.0 m/s². Halving Δt for the same Δv doubles the acceleration.
options: Dividing the same Δv by a smaller time gives a larger result, not a smaller one.
Acceleration is how fast the velocity changes, so the time matters.
Right: the same Δv in half the time doubles Δv/Δt (4.0 m/s² against 2.0 m/s²).
The time is halved, not quartered, and it is not squared in a = Δv/Δt.

items.q: A 4.5 m long car drives 2.0 km along a straight highway. Why may the car be treated as a single point when finding its average velocity?
options: In physics problems, every car is treated as having no size at all
Its length is tiny next to 2.0 km, and all its parts move together
Its mass is small compared with the mass of the road it drives on
A point model gives the car a larger average velocity than it has

why.correct: In the object model, an object is a point with a position and no size, shape or inner parts. That works when the size is small compared with the motion and all parts move together.
options: Real cars have size; the model chooses to ignore it when that does not change the answer.
Right: the object model ignores size and shape when they do not affect the motion being described.
The model is about size, shape and inner parts, not about comparing masses.
Treating the car as a point does not change its velocity; it only simplifies the description.

items.q: A runner moves around a circular track at a steady 5.0 m/s. Is the runner accelerating?
options: Yes, because the direction of the velocity keeps changing
No, because the speed does not change
No, because the runner ends each lap where it began
Yes, because 5.0 m/s is a large speed

why.correct: An object accelerates whenever its velocity changes, in size or in direction. Running around a curve changes the direction.
options: Right: velocity is a vector. A change in direction is a change in velocity, so there is an acceleration.
A steady speed is not a steady velocity when the direction changes.
Ending where you started gives zero displacement over a lap; it says nothing about the velocity changing along the way.
Acceleration is about change in velocity, not about how large the speed is.
